segments.text: Structuralism, emerging from the linguistic theory of Ferdinand de Saussure and applied to literature from the mid-20th century onward, analyses literary texts as systems of signs whose meaning derives not from any inherent connection between word and thing, but from the differential relationships among elements within the overall linguistic and cultural system.
Core theoretical foundation.

Saussure’s foundational insight — that the linguistic sign (word) is arbitrary, deriving its meaning not from any natural connection to the thing it names but from its position within a differential system of relationships to other signs (a word means what it means partly by not being the other words around it) — was extended by structuralist critics from linguistics to literature and culture more broadly, treating narrative structures, character types, and symbolic patterns as elements within larger systems governed by underlying rules and conventions, analogous to grammar, that generate meaning through structural relationship rather than direct reference to reality.
Application to literary analysis.

Structuralist literary critics sought to identify the underlying structural patterns and conventions (analogous to a language’s grammar) that generate meaning across individual literary texts — including narrative structures common across many different specific stories (such as recurring plot functions identified in folk-tale analysis), binary oppositions structuring a text’s meaning (such as nature/culture, or order/chaos), and the conventions of genre that shape how individual texts are read and understood — treating the individual literary work less as a unique, self-contained expression of authorial intention and more as a particular instance generated by and legible through broader systems of narrative and cultural convention.
Significance and subsequent critique.

Structuralism’s emphasis on underlying systems rather than individual authorial intention or the text’s apparent direct reference to reality proved highly influential across literary and cultural studies, but also attracted the critique, articulated by post-structuralist theory (including Deconstruction, Topic 46), that structuralism’s confidence in identifying stable, underlying structural systems itself rested on unexamined assumptions about language’s capacity to generate fixed, determinate meaning — a confidence post-structuralist critics would subsequently challenge.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Structuralism, building on Saussure’s linguistic theory, treats literary meaning as generated through differential relationships among elements within a larger system, rather than through direct reference between word and thing.

Structuralist criticism identifies underlying narrative structures, binary oppositions, and generic conventions that generate meaning across individual texts, treating texts as instances of broader systems rather than unique authorial expressions.
Structuralism’s confidence in identifying stable underlying structures was subsequently challenged by post-structuralist approaches, including Deconstruction (Topic 46).

segments.text: Marxist literary criticism analyses literary texts in relation to the economic and class structures of the society that produced them, treating literature not as a politically neutral aesthetic object but as a cultural product shaped by, and often reproducing or contesting, the ideological interests of a particular economic and class order.
Core theoretical foundation.

Drawing on Marx’s broader theory of historical materialism — the claim that a society’s economic “base” (its mode of production and class relations) fundamentally shapes its cultural, political, and intellectual “superstructure,” including its literature — Marxist criticism examines how literary texts encode, reflect, or contest the ideological assumptions of the economic system and class interests that produced them, treating even texts that appear politically neutral or purely aesthetic as bearing traces of the class ideology within which they were written.
Key concepts.
Ideology

— the often unexamined, naturalised assumptions and values (about class, hierarchy, and social order) that a text may reproduce without explicit political argument, making prevailing class interests appear as simply natural or common-sensical rather than historically contingent and open to challenge;
base and superstructure

— the relationship between a society’s underlying economic structure and its cultural production, with orthodox Marxist criticism generally treating culture as substantially, though not always straightforwardly or mechanically, shaped by economic relations; and
reflection versus mediation

— ongoing debate within Marxist criticism over whether literature simply reflects existing economic and class relations relatively directly, or whether it mediates and transforms those relations through the specific, semi-autonomous demands of literary and aesthetic form.
Application and examples.

Marxist critics might examine how a novel’s plot resolution reinforces or challenges prevailing class hierarchies, how working-class characters are represented (with sympathy, condescension, or invisibility), or how a text’s formal choices (which perspectives are centred, whose interior consciousness is granted narrative attention) reflect underlying assumptions about whose experience matters — approaches directly relevant, for instance, to reading the class dynamics dramatised in Shaw’s Pygmalion (Topic 32) or the industrial working-class setting of Lawrence’s Sons and Lovers (Topic 38).
Key Takeaways

items.text: Marxist criticism analyses literature in relation to the economic and class structures of the society that produced it, examining how texts encode, reflect, or contest prevailing class ideology.

Key concepts include ideology (naturalised assumptions serving class interests), the base-superstructure relationship, and ongoing debate over whether literature simply reflects or actively mediates economic relations.
The approach is directly applicable to texts explicitly engaging class dynamics, such as Shaw’s Pygmalion or Lawrence’s Sons and Lovers.

segments.text: Deconstruction, most closely associated with the philosopher Jacques Derrida, is a mode of critical reading that seeks to expose the internal contradictions, instabilities, and unresolved tensions within a text’s own language and logic, challenging the assumption that texts possess a single, stable, fully coherent meaning.
Core theoretical foundation: the instability of language.

Deconstruction extends and radicalises Saussure’s structuralist insight (Topic 44) that meaning is generated through differential relationships between signs, arguing that this differential process never fully stabilises into fixed, determinate meaning — every sign’s meaning depends on its difference from other signs, which themselves depend on further differences, in an endless chain (Derrida’s term “différance” captures this simultaneous “differing” and perpetual “deferring” of stable meaning) that resists ever arriving at a final, self-sufficient, grounding meaning outside this endless referential chain.
Method: locating and exploiting internal textual contradiction.

Deconstructive reading characteristically identifies binary oppositions structuring a text’s apparent argument (such as speech/writing, presence/absence, reason/emotion) and demonstrates that the privileged, seemingly primary term in each opposition actually depends on, and cannot be fully separated from, the supposedly secondary, subordinate term — showing that the text’s own language undermines the very hierarchy or stable meaning it appears to assert, revealing what deconstructive critics call the text’s internal “aporia” (an irresolvable point of contradiction or undecidability) rather than a single, coherent, intended meaning.
Significance and critique.

Deconstruction proved highly influential, and controversial, across literary studies from the 1970s onward, prized by advocates for its rigorous attentiveness to language’s actual complexity and its challenge to naively confident claims of stable textual meaning, while critics have charged the approach with a tendency toward excessive interpretive relativism, obscure or unnecessarily difficult prose style, and, in some applications, a neglect of a text’s historical and social context in favour of purely internal linguistic analysis — a criticism that motivated subsequent critical approaches (including some strands of Marxist, feminist, and postcolonial criticism, Topics 45, 48–49) to insist on reconnecting textual analysis more directly to historical and social context.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Deconstruction, following Derrida, argues that language’s differential structure never fully stabilises into fixed meaning, since every sign’s meaning depends on an endless chain of further differences.

Its characteristic method identifies binary oppositions structuring a text’s argument and demonstrates that the privileged term actually depends on the subordinate one, revealing internal textual contradiction (“aporia”) rather than stable, coherent meaning.

While influential for its rigorous attentiveness to linguistic complexity, deconstruction has been criticised for interpretive relativism and neglect of historical/social context, prompting subsequent approaches to reconnect textual analysis to context more directly.

segments.text: Psychoanalytic literary criticism applies concepts from Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalytic theory (and later theorists building on or revising Freud, including Jacques Lacan) to interpret literary texts, treating them as expressions of unconscious psychological processes, whether attributed to characters, authors, or readers.
Core Freudian concepts applied to literature.
The unconscious

— the theory that much psychological life operates below conscious awareness, meaning a text’s manifest content (what is explicitly stated) may conceal latent, unconsciously encoded meaning, analogous to Freud’s analysis of dreams;
repression and symptom

— psychologically threatening material may be repressed from conscious awareness but return indirectly, in disguised or symbolic form, within a text’s imagery, plot structure, or characters’ seemingly inexplicable behaviour; and
the Oedipus complex

— Freud’s theory of a child’s unconscious rivalrous desire toward the same-sex parent and desire for the opposite-sex parent, a framework frequently applied directly to texts dramatising intense, psychologically fraught parent-child relationships, such as D. H. Lawrence’s Sons and Lovers (Topic 38), whose central dynamic has been read almost paradigmatically through this Freudian lens.
Objects of psychoanalytic analysis.

Psychoanalytic criticism can be directed at several distinct objects: the psychology of fictional characters (treating them, provisionally, as if they possessed a genuine unconscious psychological life amenable to analysis); the psychology of the author (reading a text as expressing the author’s own unconscious psychological conflicts, an approach of particular relevance to strongly autobiographical works like Sons and Lovers or Joyce’s Portrait of the Artist discussed in Topic 40); or, in later reader-response-influenced psychoanalytic criticism, the psychology of the reading process itself, examining how texts engage and gratify (or frustrate) unconscious reader desires and anxieties.
Significance and critique.

Psychoanalytic criticism has proven particularly generative for analysing texts dealing explicitly with desire, family conflict, repression, and symbolic or dream-like imagery, but has attracted criticism for sometimes imposing a predetermined interpretive framework (Freudian concepts assumed valid in advance) onto texts regardless of their specific historical and cultural context, and for treating fictional characters as if they possessed the kind of coherent, analysable unconscious psychology properly belonging only to actual individual human minds.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Psychoanalytic criticism applies Freudian concepts — the unconscious, repression and symbolic return, and the Oedipus complex — to interpret literary texts as expressions of unconscious psychological processes.
Analysis can be directed at fictional characters, the author’s own psychology (particularly relevant to autobiographical works like Sons and Lovers), or the reading process itself.
The approach has proven generative for texts dealing with desire and family conflict but has been criticised for imposing a predetermined interpretive framework regardless of historical context.

segments.text: Feminist literary criticism examines how literary texts represent, construct, and sometimes challenge gender roles and the social position of women, and critically interrogates the historical exclusion or marginalisation of women writers from the literary canon and critical establishment.
Major strands and concerns.
Representation of women in literature

— examining how female characters are constructed, particularly by male authors, and whether they are granted full psychological complexity and narrative agency or reduced to limited, stereotyped roles serving male protagonists’ development (a concern directly relevant to reading Tennyson’s “The Lady of Shalott,” Topic 14, or the constrained position of women across much canonical literature);
recovery of women writers

— feminist criticism has been instrumental in recovering and re-evaluating women writers historically neglected or marginalised by a predominantly male-defined literary canon and critical establishment, and in examining the specific material and social obstacles (education, economic independence, publishing access) that historically constrained women’s literary production; and
gynocriticism

— a term coined by Elaine Showalter for criticism focused specifically on women’s writing as a distinct literary tradition, examining recurring themes, forms, and concerns across women authors’ work considered on its own terms rather than measured against a male-defined literary standard.
Theoretical development: from Anglo-American to French feminist theory.

Feminist criticism developed along somewhat distinct lines in different critical traditions — an Anglo-American tradition tending toward more historically and sociologically grounded analysis of women’s actual literary representation and production, and a French feminist tradition (including theorists like Hélène Cixous and Luce Irigaray) drawing more heavily on psychoanalytic and post-structuralist theory (Topics 46–47) to examine how language and symbolic systems themselves may be structured around implicitly masculine norms, with some French feminist theorists proposing the possibility of a distinctly feminine mode of writing (“écriture féminine”) that might challenge or exceed these masculine linguistic norms.
Application.

Feminist criticism offers a particularly productive lens for analysing texts across this subject’s curriculum, from the constrained, ultimately fatal isolation of Tennyson’s Lady of Shalott (Topic 14), to Hardy’s independent-minded Bathsheba Everdene (Topic 37), to the specific historical and material conditions shaping women’s authorship more broadly.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Feminist criticism examines the representation of women in literary texts, works to recover historically marginalised women writers, and, through gynocriticism, analyses women’s writing as a distinct literary tradition on its own terms.

The field developed along both an Anglo-American tradition emphasising historical and sociological analysis and a French feminist tradition drawing on psychoanalytic and post-structuralist theory to examine language’s implicitly masculine structuring.

The approach offers a productive lens across diverse texts, from the constrained female figures of canonical poetry and fiction to the material conditions historically shaping women’s literary production.

segments.text: Postcolonial criticism examines literature produced in the context of European colonialism and its aftermath — analysing how colonial power relations are represented, reinforced, or resisted in literary texts, and giving particular critical attention to the voices, perspectives, and literary traditions of formerly colonised peoples.
Core concerns.
Representation of the colonised “Other”

— building substantially on Edward Said’s foundational concept of “Orientalism” (the analysis of how Western literary and scholarly texts historically constructed the non-European world as an exotic, inferior, or threatening “Other” against which a superior European identity was implicitly defined), postcolonial criticism examines how colonial-era literature represents colonised peoples and cultures, often revealing embedded assumptions of European superiority even in texts not explicitly or intentionally engaged in colonial political argument;
the “writing back” tradition

— postcolonial criticism gives particular attention to literature by formerly colonised writers that directly responds to, revises, or challenges canonical Western texts and their representational assumptions, reclaiming narrative authority over stories and perspectives colonial-era literature had appropriated or distorted; and
hybridity and cultural identity

— drawing on theorists including Homi Bhabha, postcolonial criticism examines the complex, often unstable cultural identities produced by colonial contact, in which colonised (and, to a lesser extent, colonising) cultures are transformed through mutual, asymmetrical influence rather than remaining in simple, separate, unmixed cultural isolation.
Application to canonical literature.

Postcolonial criticism can be productively applied even to texts not explicitly concerned with colonialism, examining how imperial assumptions and hierarchies shape texts’ underlying worldview — for example, examining the largely unexamined imperial and racial assumptions embedded within much 19th-century English fiction, or, in Eliot’s case (Topics 17–18), examining how “The Waste Land”’s incorporation of non-Western religious and mythological material (Buddhist and Hindu scripture) reflects a particular, historically situated relationship between Western Modernism and non-Western cultural material.
Significance.

Postcolonial criticism has been instrumental in expanding the literary canon studied in English-language literary education beyond a narrowly British and American frame, and in developing critical vocabulary for analysing power, representation, and cultural exchange across colonial and postcolonial contexts — a critical framework of particular relevance and significance for literary study in Pakistan specifically, given the country’s own direct historical relationship to British colonial rule and its ongoing negotiation of linguistic and literary identity across English and indigenous literary traditions.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Postcolonial criticism examines how colonial power relations are represented, reinforced, or resisted in literature, drawing substantially on Edward Said’s concept of “Orientalism” and its analysis of how Western texts construct the colonised world as an inferior “Other.”

The “writing back” tradition examines literature by formerly colonised writers directly responding to and revising canonical Western texts, while hybridity theory examines the complex, unstable cultural identities produced by colonial contact.

The approach has expanded the literary canon beyond a narrowly British/American frame and holds particular relevance for Pakistani literary study, given the country’s direct historical relationship to British colonial rule.
